title: Comparison and ratio tests
objectives: Prove and use the comparison, ratio and integral tests.

screens.title: Rising, with a ceiling
screens.prose: In `taylor` you used the comparison test without a proof. This level proves the tests. The lower dots are the partial sums $T_n$ of $\sum \tfrac{1}{2^n + n}$. The upper ones are $B_n$ of $\sum \tfrac{1}{2^n}$, which tend to 1. Slide $n$.
screens.question: Each term $\tfrac{1}{2^n + n}$ is positive and below $\tfrac{1}{2^n}$. What must $T_n$ do as $n \to \infty$?

options.text: Converge, to a limit of at most 1: $T_n$ rises and never passes 1.
Tend to 1, like $B_n$.
options.why: You matched the ceiling. A rising sequence below 1 converges to its supremum, which can sit below 1; here about 0.6973.

options.text: We cannot tell without a formula for $T_n$.
options.why: You looked for a formula. Rising and bounded is enough: that is the monotone convergence theorem from level 2.

options.text: Pass 1 eventually, since it never stops rising.
options.why: You let rising mean unbounded. Each $T_n$ is below $B_n$, and every $B_n$ is below 1.

hints.text: Compare each blue dot with the dot above it.
$T_n \le B_n < 1$ for every $n$.
Rising and bounded above: level 2's monotone convergence theorem applies.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask two things of $T_n$: does it rise, and is it capped?

explain.text: Positive terms make $T_n$ rise, and $T_n \le B_n < 1$ caps it. Monotone convergence gives a limit, about 0.6973. Nothing else about the terms was needed.

screens.title: Why the sums rise
screens.prose: In general let $0 \le a_n \le b_n$ for every $n$, with $\sum b_n = B$. Write $T_n = a_1 + \cdots + a_n$ and $B_n = b_1 + \cdots + b_n$.
screens.question: Why is $(T_n)$ increasing?

options.text: Because $a_n \le b_n$.
options.why: You used the comparison. Rising needs only that each new term is at least 0; the comparison is for the bound.

options.text: Because $a_n \to 0$.
options.why: You used the size of the terms. Terms tending to 0 can be negative, and then the sums fall.

options.text: Because $\sum b_n$ converges.
options.why: You used the other series. Whether $T_n$ rises depends only on the signs of the $a_n$.

hints.text: What is $T_{n+1} - T_n$?
It is the new term, $a_{n+1}$.
Every $a_n \ge 0$.

feedback.correct: Right. Non-negative terms make the partial sums rise.

explain.text: $T_{n+1} = T_n + a_{n+1}$ and $a_{n+1} \ge 0$. So each partial sum is at least the one before. This is the first half of what monotone convergence needs.

screens.title: Why the sums are capped
screens.prose: In general let $0 \le a_n \le b_n$ for every $n$, with $\sum b_n = B$. Write $T_n = a_1 + \cdots + a_n$ and $B_n = b_1 + \cdots + b_n$. Now we bound $T_n$.
screens.question: Why is $T_n \le B$ for every $n$?

options.text: $T_n \le B_n \le B$: add $a_k \le b_k$ for $k \le n$, and $(B_n)$ rises to its limit $B$.
$T_n \le b_n$, and $b_n \le B$.
options.why: You compared a total with one term. $T_n$ adds $n$ terms; compare it with $B_n$, which adds the matching $n$.

options.text: $T_n \le B_n$ and $B_n \to B$, so $T_n \to B$.
options.why: You read a limit off an inequality. $T_n \le B_n$ caps $T_n$; it does not make the two limits equal.

options.text: $T_n \le 1$, because every $a_n \le 1$.
options.why: You bounded the terms, not the sum. A thousand terms of size $\tfrac12$ add to 500.

hints.text: Add the inequalities $a_k \le b_k$ for $k = 1$ to $n$.
That gives $T_n \le B_n$.
Each $b_k \ge 0$, so $(B_n)$ increases, and an increasing sequence stays below its limit.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $T_n$ with the partial sum $B_n$, then $B_n$ with $B$.

explain.text: Adding $a_k \le b_k$ gives $T_n \le B_n$. Because every $b_k \ge 0$, $(B_n)$ rises to $B$, so $B_n \le B$. Hence $B$ is an upper bound for every $T_n$.

screens.title: The comparison test proved
screens.prose: Assemble the proof that $0 \le a_n \le b_n$ and $\sum b_n$ convergent give $\sum a_n$ convergent. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Let $T_n = a_1 + \cdots + a_n$, $B_n = b_1 + \cdots + b_n$ and $B = \sum b_n$.
$T_{n+1} = T_n + a_{n+1} \ge T_n$, so $(T_n)$ is increasing.
$T_n \le B_n \le B$, since $a_k \le b_k$ and $(B_n)$ increases to $B$.
By the monotone convergence theorem, $(T_n)$ converges, so $\sum a_n$ converges. $\blacksquare$
Since $T_n \le B_n$ and $B_n \to B$, we get $\sum a_n = B$.
lines.why: You equated the sums. The bound gives $\sum a_n \le B$; here $0.6973 < 1$.

lines.text: Since $a_n \le b_n \to 0$, the terms tend to 0, so $\sum a_n$ converges.
lines.why: You used terms tending to 0. That is necessary, not enough: $\sum \tfrac1n$.

hints.text: Name the partial sums, then show the two facts monotone convergence needs.
The two facts are: increasing, and bounded above. Either may come first.
Order: set up, increasing and bounded (either order), then monotone convergence.

feedback.correct: Right. Increasing and bounded, so convergent.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Prove rising and capped, then quote monotone convergence.

byKey.d1: You concluded $\sum a_n = B$. Comparison bounds the sum; it does not pin it.
byKey.d2: You argued from $a_n \to 0$, which $\sum \tfrac1n$ shows is not enough.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Rising comes from $a_n \ge 0$ and the cap from $a_n \le b_n$. Monotone convergence then gives a limit, at most $B$. Completeness, through level 2, does the real work.

screens.title: The other half
screens.prose: Now let $0 \le a_n \le b_n$ with $\sum a_n$ divergent. For example $\tfrac1n \le \tfrac{n+1}{n^2}$, and $\sum \tfrac1n$ diverges.
screens.question: Why must $\sum \tfrac{n+1}{n^2}$ diverge?

options.text: If it converged, the first half would make $\sum \tfrac1n$ converge. It does not, so $\sum \tfrac{n+1}{n^2}$ diverges.
Because its terms do not tend to 0.
options.why: You used the term test. Here $\tfrac{n+1}{n^2} \to 0$, so that test is silent.

options.text: It need not: comparison only ever proves convergence.
options.why: You kept one half. The contrapositive of the first half proves divergence of the larger series.

options.text: Because its terms are larger, so its sum is larger than $\sum \tfrac1n$.
options.why: You compared two sums that do not exist. The argument must avoid naming a value for a divergent series.

hints.text: Suppose the larger series converged. What would the first half give?
It would make the smaller series, $\sum \tfrac1n$, converge.
That contradicts l11, so the larger one diverges.

feedback.correct: Right. Divergence passes upwards, by the contrapositive.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Assume the larger series converges and apply the first half.

explain.text: The first half says: larger convergent forces smaller convergent. Its contrapositive says: smaller divergent forces larger divergent. So $\sum \tfrac{n+1}{n^2}$ diverges.

screens.title: Room below 1
screens.prose: The ratio test: $a_n > 0$ and $\tfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \to L < 1$. Take $\sum \tfrac{n}{2^n}$, with ratios $\tfrac{n+1}{2n} \to L = \tfrac12$. The proof sets $r = \tfrac{L+1}{2} = \tfrac34$.
screens.question: Why is there an $N$ with $\tfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} < r$ for every $n \ge N$?

options.text: Because $r > L$: the limit definition with $\varepsilon = r - L = \tfrac14$ gives such an $N$; here $N = 3$.
Because every ratio is already below 1.
options.why: You used each ratio. Ratios below 1 can creep up to 1, as $\left(\tfrac{n}{n+1}\right)^2$ do; we need one fixed $r < 1$.

options.text: Take $r = L$ instead: the ratios tend to $L$.
options.why: You left no room. The ratios can stay above $L$ for ever, as $\tfrac{n+1}{2n} > \tfrac12$ does.

options.text: Any $r < 1$ works, for example $r = \tfrac14$.
options.why: You picked $r$ below $L$. The ratios approach $\tfrac12$, so they are eventually above $\tfrac14$.

hints.text: $r$ sits strictly between $L$ and 1.
Use $\varepsilon = r - L$ in the definition of $\tfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \to L$.
Here $\tfrac{n+1}{2n} - \tfrac12 = \tfrac{1}{2n} < \tfrac14$ exactly when $n > 2$.

feedback.correct: Right. The gap $r - L$ is the $\varepsilon$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the definition of the limit with $\varepsilon = r - L$.

explain.text: Since $r - L > 0$, the definition of the limit gives $N$ with $\tfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} < L + (r - L) = r$ for $n \ge N$. For $\sum \tfrac{n}{2^n}$, $\tfrac{1}{2n} < \tfrac14$ from $n = 3$. Halfway between $L$ and 1 is simply a safe choice.

screens.title: The ratio test proved
screens.prose: Assemble the proof that $a_n > 0$ and $\tfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \to L < 1$ give $\sum a_n$ convergent. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: With $\varepsilon = r - L$, there is $N$ with $\tfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} < r$ for every $n \ge N$.
By induction on $k$, $a_{N+k} \le a_N r^k$ for every $k \ge 0$.
$\sum_{k \ge 0} a_N r^k$ is geometric with $0 < r < 1$, so it converges.
By comparison $\sum_{k \ge 0} a_{N+k}$ converges, and the first $N - 1$ terms do not change that. $\blacksquare$
So $a_{n+1} < a_n$ for $n \ge N$, and a series of decreasing positive terms converges.
lines.why: You used decreasing terms. $\tfrac1n$ decreases and $\sum \tfrac1n$ diverges; the geometric bound does the work.

lines.text: Let $r = L$, so that $a_{N+k} \le a_N L^k$.
lines.why: You left no room between the ratios and $L$. The ratios may stay above $L$ for ever.

hints.text: Fix $r$ first, then find $N$ from the limit.
Multiplying $\tfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} < r$ from $N$ to $N + k - 1$ gives $a_{N+k} < a_N r^k$.
Order: choose $r$, find $N$, the geometric bound, the geometric sum, then comparison.

feedback.correct: Right. Past $N$ the series sits under a geometric one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose $r$ between $L$ and 1, find $N$, bound the tail by $a_N r^k$, then compare.

byKey.d1: You used decreasing terms. That is not enough, as $\sum \tfrac1n$ shows.
byKey.d2: You took $r = L$. The proof needs room above $L$, and still below 1.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Past $N$ each term is less than $r$ times the one before, so the tail sits under $a_N(1 + r + r^2 + \cdots)$. The comparison test finishes the proof. For $\sum \tfrac{n}{2^n}$ the sum is 2, since $S - \tfrac12 S = \sum \tfrac{1}{2^n} = 1$.

screens.title: A ratio that tends to $\tfrac1e$
screens.prose: For $a_n = \tfrac{n!}{n^n}$ the ratio simplifies: $$\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} = \frac{(n+1)!}{(n+1)^{n+1}} \cdot \frac{n^n}{n!} = \left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^n.$$ The dots are these ratios.
screens.question: Fill in the ratios to four decimal places, the limit, and the verdict.

hints.text: $\left(\tfrac{10}{11}\right)^{10}$: raise $0.90909$ to the tenth power.
$\tfrac1e \approx 0.3679$, the dashed line.
$L \approx 0.3679 < 1$, so the ratio test gives convergence.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute each ratio, then compare the limit with 1.

byKey.r5c1: $L = \tfrac1e < 1$, so the ratio test proves convergence.

explain.text: $\left(\tfrac{n}{n+1}\right)^n = \left(1 + \tfrac1n\right)^{-n} \to \tfrac1e \approx 0.3679$. The ratios fall towards it: 0.3855 at 10, 0.3697 at 100. Since $L < 1$, the series converges, to about 1.8799.

screens.title: Rectangles and a curve
screens.prose: Each term $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$ is the area of a width-1 rectangle of height $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$. The curve is $y = \tfrac{1}{x^2}$, which falls. Switch between the two ways of placing the rectangles.

state.caption: Rectangle on $[k-1, k]$ with height $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$, for $k = 2$ to 6.

frames.caption: Rectangle on $[k-1, k]$ with height $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$, for $k = 2$ to 6.
Rectangle on $[k, k+1]$ with height $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$, for $k = 1$ to 5.

screens.question: Which rectangles lie under the curve?

options.text: The ones on $[k-1, k]$: there the curve is at least $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$, its value at the right end.
The ones on $[k, k+1]$: there the curve starts at $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$.
options.why: You looked at the left end only. The curve falls below $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$ after $x = k$, so these rectangles stick out above it.

options.text: Both: every rectangle touches the curve.
options.why: You took touching for lying under. A rectangle on $[k, k+1]$ touches at $x = k$ and is above the curve everywhere else.

options.text: Neither: the rectangles always poke out somewhere.
options.why: Check the rectangle on $[1, 2]$ of height $\tfrac14$. The curve is above $\tfrac14$ for every $x < 2$.

hints.text: The curve falls. On an interval, where is it lowest?
On $[k-1, k]$ the lowest value is $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$, at the right end.
So the rectangle of height $\tfrac{1}{k^2}$ on $[k-1, k]$ fits under the curve.

feedback.correct: Right. Height from the right end fits under a falling curve.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the curve's lowest point on each interval.

explain.text: The rectangles on $[k-1, k]$ sit under the curve, so $\sum_{k > m} \tfrac{1}{k^2} \le \int_m^\infty \tfrac{dx}{x^2} = \tfrac1m$. The others sit above, so the same tail is at least $\int_{m+1}^\infty \tfrac{dx}{x^2} = \tfrac{1}{m+1}$. With $x^{-p}$ the same picture gives the **integral test**: $\sum \tfrac{1}{n^p}$ converges exactly when $p > 1$.

canvas.caption: Both sets: the lower rectangles sit under the curve, the taller ones above it.

screens.title: Below a divergent series
screens.prose: A classmate proves that $\sum \tfrac{1}{2n}$ diverges. The conclusion is true. One line proves nothing.

rows: A series of non-negative terms below a divergent series diverges.

screens.question: Tap the line that is false.

hints.text: Test each line's claim on another pair of series.
Line 3 would also apply to $\tfrac{1}{n^2} \le \tfrac1n$.
$\sum \tfrac1{n^2}$ converges, so line 3 is false.

feedback.correct: Right. Lying below a divergent series proves nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try each line's rule on $\tfrac{1}{n^2} \le \tfrac1n$.

byKey.r1: Line 2 is true: the grouping proof of l11.
byKey.r3: Line 4 is true, as it happens. It does not follow from the lines above it, because line 3 is false.

explain.text: Line 3 would also give $\sum \tfrac{1}{n^2}$ divergent, since $\tfrac1{n^2} \le \tfrac1n$; but it converges. Divergence passes upwards only, from a smaller series to a larger one. An honest proof: the partial sums are $\tfrac12 H_n$, which are unbounded.

screens.title: Trapping the sum
screens.prose: The tail after $S_n$ lies between $\tfrac{1}{n+1}$ and $\tfrac1n$. Write `sum_with_bounds(n)`, returning $(S_n, S_n + \tfrac{1}{n+1}, S_n + \tfrac1n)$ for $\sum \tfrac1{k^2}$.
screens.question: Complete the function.

widget.starter:
import math

def sum_with_bounds(n):
    """(S_n, S_n + 1/(n+1), S_n + 1/n) for the series 1/k^2."""
    ...

tests.call: all(sum_with_bounds(n)[1] < math.pi ** 2 / 6 < sum_with_bounds(n)[2] for n in range(1, 200))

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. Values are compared with math.isclose within absolute 1e-9. The last two check two things. One is that pi^2/6 lies strictly between the bounds for every n below 200. The other is that three values come back.

hints.text: Add `1 / k ** 2` for `k` from 1 to `n`.
Then add $\tfrac{1}{n+1}$ for the lower bound and $\tfrac1n$ for the upper.
Return the three numbers as a tuple: `(s, s + 1 / (n + 1), s + 1 / n)`.

feedback.correct: Right. At $n = 10$ the bounds are 1.640677 and 1.649768.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the order: $S_n$, then $S_n + \tfrac{1}{n+1}$, then $S_n + \tfrac1n$.

explain.text: At $n = 10$, $S_{10} \approx 1.549768$ and the bounds are 1.640677 and 1.649768. Both trap $\tfrac{\pi^2}{6} \approx 1.644934$, a fact Euler proved. Ten terms and a picture pin the sum to within 0.01.

screens.title: How many jumps to price
screens.prose: A Merton jump-diffusion call price is $\sum_{n \ge 0} w_n C_n$. Here $w_n = e^{-\lambda T}\tfrac{(\lambda T)^n}{n!}$ is the chance of $n$ jumps. Each $C_n$ is a Black-Scholes price, at most the spot, £100. Take $\lambda T = 2$. The bars are the $w_n$.

state.caption: $w_{10} \approx 3.8 \times 10^{-5}$: the last bars are too small to see.

screens.question: The weights after $n = 10$ add to about $8.3 \times 10^{-6}$. At most how much, in £, can those terms add to the price?

hints.text: Each dropped term is $w_n C_n \le w_n \times 100$.
So the dropped terms add at most $100 \sum_{n > 10} w_n$.

feedback.correct: Right. Under a tenth of a penny.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bound each $C_n$ by £100 and add the weights you drop.

byKey.pct: You gave the answer in pence. In pounds it is 0.00083.
byKey.weight: You gave the dropped weight, not money. Multiply by the £100 bound on each price.

explain.text: The ratio $\tfrac{w_{n+1}}{w_n} = \tfrac{\lambda T}{n+1} \to 0$, so the series converges for any $\lambda T$. With $\lambda T = 2$ the weights past 10 total about $8.3 \times 10^{-6}$, so the dropped terms are under £0.001. That is why a library stops at about 10 terms.

ideas: Comparison: if $0 \le a_n \le b_n$ and $\sum b_n$ converges, the partial sums of $\sum a_n$ rise and are capped, so converge. Divergence passes upwards.
Ratio: if $\tfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \to L < 1$, past some $N$ the terms sit under $a_N r^k$ with $r = \tfrac{L+1}{2}$. $L = 1$ decides nothing.
Integral: rectangles put $\sum_{n > m} \tfrac{1}{n^2}$ between $\tfrac{1}{m+1}$ and $\tfrac1m$; $\sum \tfrac{1}{n^p}$ converges exactly when $p > 1$.

formula.name: Ratio test
formula.note: Geometric comparison past $N$; $L = 1$ needs another test.

summary.trap: Being below a divergent series proves nothing: $\tfrac{1}{n^2} \le \tfrac1n$, and $\sum \tfrac1{n^2}$ converges.

quiz.prose: For $\sum \tfrac1n$ the ratios are $\tfrac{n}{n+1} \to 1$. For $\sum \tfrac{1}{n^2}$ they are $\left(\tfrac{n}{n+1}\right)^2 \to 1$.
quiz.question: What does the ratio test conclude when $L = 1$?

options.text: Nothing: $L = 1$ for one series that diverges and one that converges.
Convergence, since every ratio is below 1.
options.why: You used each ratio. They creep up to 1, and $\sum \tfrac1n$ diverges.

options.text: Divergence, since the ratios reach 1.
options.why: You read $L = 1$ as $L > 1$. $\sum \tfrac{1}{n^2}$ has $L = 1$ and converges.

options.text: Slow convergence.
options.why: You read $L$ as a speed. With $L = 1$ the test gives no verdict at all.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two series: same $L$, different fates.

explain.text: Both series have $L = 1$, yet $\sum \tfrac1n$ diverges and $\sum \tfrac1{n^2}$ converges. So $L = 1$ cannot decide. Comparison or the integral test settle such cases.

quiz.prose: The ratio test shows $S = \sum_{n \ge 1} \tfrac{n}{2^n}$ converges. Now $S - \tfrac12 S = \tfrac12 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac18 + \cdots$, by shifting the terms of $\tfrac12 S$ one place.
quiz.question: What is $S$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sum the geometric series on the right, then solve for $S$.

byKey.ratio: You gave $L = \tfrac12$, the ratio limit. The question asks for the sum.

explain.text: $S - \tfrac12 S = \sum_{n \ge 1} \tfrac{1}{2^n} = 1$, so $\tfrac12 S = 1$ and $S = 2$. The subtraction is allowed because $S$ converges, which the ratio test proved. Check: $S_{10} = \tfrac{509}{256} \approx 1.9883$.

quiz.question: What does the comparison test say about $\sum \tfrac{1}{n^2 + n}$?

options.text: It converges, with sum at most 1.6449. In fact the sum is 1, by l11.
It converges, with sum $\tfrac{\pi^2}{6}$.
options.why: You equated the sums. Comparison gives only $\sum a_n \le \sum b_n$; here $1 < 1.6449$.

options.text: Nothing, because it lies below a series.
options.why: You remembered the trap the wrong way round. Lying below a convergent series is exactly what proves convergence.

options.text: It converges, with sum above 1.6449.
options.why: You reversed the inequality. Smaller terms give a smaller sum.

feedback.correct: Right. Below a convergent series, so convergent.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which way does the comparison point, and what does it give?

explain.text: Smaller non-negative terms than a convergent series give a convergent series. The bound on the sum is $\tfrac{\pi^2}{6}$, not equality. Telescoping gives the exact value, 1.

quiz.prose: Take $\sum \tfrac{1}{n^{1.1}}$. Its ratios tend to 1. The integral $\int_1^\infty x^{-1.1}\,dx = 10$.
quiz.question: Does it converge?

options.text: Yes: $p = 1.1 > 1$, and the rectangles give $\sum \tfrac{1}{n^{1.1}} \le 1 + 10 = 11$.
No: the ratio test gives $L = 1$.
options.why: You read $L = 1$ as divergence. It is no verdict; the integral test decides.

options.text: No: $n^{1.1}$ is too close to $n$.
options.why: You judged by eye. Any $p > 1$ gives a finite integral, so the series converges, if slowly.

options.text: Yes, and its sum is 10.
options.why: You equated the sum with the integral. The integral bounds the tail; the sum is between 10 and 11.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the integral test with $p = 1.1$.

explain.text: The rectangles under $x^{-1.1}$ give $\sum_{n \ge 2} n^{-1.1} \le \int_1^\infty x^{-1.1}\,dx = 10$. So the partial sums are below 11 and rise, hence converge. Every $p > 1$ works the same way.
